name: Left-wing populism
summary: Left-wing populism is a political strategy that builds a collective 'people' out of heterogeneous democratic demands against an 'oligarchy' of financial and political power, in the name of equality and popular sovereignty. Its theorists (Laclau, Mouffe) treat it as a discursive strategy rather than a programme, and scholars place it as the inclusionary strand of populism, opposed to the ethnic 'people' of the radical right. It rejects the post-political consensus and neoliberalism while keeping liberal-democratic institutions and the left/right distinction.

scope: The 21st-century strand described by Mouffe as a discursive strategy of building a 'people' against an 'oligarchy' to radicalise democracy, grounded in Laclau's discourse theory, and by Mudde and Rovira Kaltwasser and by Stavrakakis and Katsambekis as the inclusionary strand of populism. Party platforms (Podemos, Syriza, La France Insoumise) and the 1892 Omaha Platform are not used as sources. It excludes right-wing populism and, as separate subjects, Latin American nationalist-populist regimes.
